title: Victory and Catastrophe
subtitle: An unfinished campaign and the beginning of the Babyn Yar massacre
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: Germany prepared another offensive as the Moscow supply conference opened and the murder of Kiev’s Jews began. The phase closes by examining continuing military limits and the escalation of organised killing under occupation.
body:
Two consequences of conquest

On 29 September 1941, Jewish families in Kiev were obeying an assembly order backed by the threat of death. They brought documents, money and clothing, possessions consistent with the removal many expected. German authorities were directing them towards Babyn Yar. Elsewhere, formations released from the Kiev battle were preparing another offensive, this time towards Moscow. The military victory had produced both an opportunity to attack again and power over an occupied population. The decisions made with that power cannot be understood through battlefield success alone. [1][2]

The five weeks covered by this phase had transformed the military situation. Leningrad’s principal land connection with the Soviet interior had been severed; the German salient at Yelnya had been evacuated under Soviet pressure; and the Southwestern Front had suffered a catastrophic encirclement. None of those outcomes can simply stand for the entire campaign. Germany had won an enormous battle in the south without defeating the Soviet Union. The Red Army had achieved a local success in the centre without removing the danger to Moscow. Leningrad remained Soviet, but its survival now depended on a supply problem of exceptional severity.[3]a

The advance placed territory and people under institutions able to organise mass murder. German military difficulties did not prevent those institutions from committing personnel and administrative effort to killing. Their decisions belong within the consequences of conquest for the people brought under German power. An assessment confined to the next operational opportunity would leave out what the victory was already making possible.

The northern objective remains beyond reach

By the end of September, Army Group North had isolated Leningrad from its main overland supply routes without capturing the city. The loss of Shlisselburg on 8 September remained decisive because it closed the connection along the southern side of Lake Ladoga. The Soviet position still included access to the lake, but access alone could not feed a metropolis and its defending armies. Cargo required a route to the eastern shore, vessels and loading facilities for the crossing, and transport onward from the western shore. Each stage imposed a separate limit on what could actually reach the people who needed it.[3][4]

The transport problem examined in Leningrad Cut Off had not been solved by the first lake deliveries. The September water route preserved contact with the interior, but it did not restore the capacity of the lost overland system. By the end of the month, German policy made that shortfall more dangerous: the leadership intended to exploit isolation to destroy the city. The later winter catastrophe remained ahead, but its history already included a functioning yet inadequate supply route and a deliberate decision to deny protection to the inhabitants.

Finland’s positions on the Karelian Isthmus and Svir added pressure without completing a continuous line with the Germans at Shlisselburg. The intervening territory preserved the Soviet lake connection. Finnish command and political objectives remained distinct from those of Army Group North, even where their operations restricted the same Soviet options. This geography was essential to Leningrad’s continued communication with the interior.[3]b

German policy had also become explicit. The directive of 22 September, later introduced at Nuremberg as document C-124, envisaged enclosing and destroying Leningrad while refusing responsibility for feeding its population, even in the event of surrender. By 29 September, the instruction formed part of the documented German policy governing the treatment of a city whose supply connections had already been gravely restricted. It turns the supply crisis into more than an accidental consequence of interrupted communications. German leaders intended to exploit the population’s vulnerability. The subsequent winter catastrophe still lay ahead, but the policy that made civilian starvation an instrument of conquest was already present.[5]c

At the same time, the transfer of mobile forces towards Army Group Centre constrained what the northern command could attempt next. The choice to concentrate for Moscow did not eliminate Leningrad as an objective; it changed the balance between assault, containment and future operations around the lake. Resources committed to one strategic aim were unavailable elsewhere. This continuing redistribution is a better explanation of the front’s development than the assumption that every German army group advanced with a permanently adequate and independent allocation of strength.[3]d

Yelnya, Kiev and the unfinished southern campaign

In the centre, the Soviet recapture of Yelnya in early September had removed a German salient and demonstrated that sustained attacks could compel a withdrawal. It had not destroyed Army Group Centre or secured the approaches to Moscow. The German command was now bringing mobile formations back into that theatre and reinforcing them from elsewhere. The experience at Yelnya therefore belonged to a continuing contest in which local success and strategic danger coexisted. Its defenders and attackers had learned something about the cost of concentrated fighting; neither side had been released from the consequences of losses already incurred.[3]e

The victory around Kiev altered the southern balance more radically. Much of the Southwestern Front had ceased to exist as an organised force, and German armies could prepare to move towards new objectives beyond the Dnieper. Yet the end of the pocket battle did not make the whole southern theatre available for unrestricted exploitation. The U.S. Army campaign study describes continued operations towards Kharkov and the southern approaches while forces were also required at the entrance to the Crimea. Movement to those objectives depended upon the condition of the formations emerging from the previous operation and upon the supply routes behind them.[1]

Odessa still resisted on 29 September. Romanian forces had not taken it quickly and needed German assistance. Its continued defence tied down troops after the larger front had moved far to the east. Access by sea also made its situation different from the Kiev pocket: an enclosing land front did not cut every connection. The southern campaign contained these unfinished operations alongside Germany’s major victory.[1]

Manstein’s 11th Army faced a separate obstacle at the Perekop Isthmus, the narrow approach into Crimea. The U.S. Army campaign study records an attempted breakthrough on 26 September; the peninsula’s campaign remained unfinished at the end of the month. The Kiev victory did not remove the need to force this defended entrance or meet Soviet pressure elsewhere. Those tasks continued to demand German and allied troops.[1][3]f

These differences explain why the phase ends with an assessment rather than a single verdict on momentum. German operational success was real, Soviet losses were severe, and further German advances remained possible. The defending state nevertheless retained armies outside the destroyed pocket, an industrial system being reorganised and the ability to create new formations. The important question was how quickly those resources could become effective military power. Possessing manpower somewhere in the Soviet Union did not mean that trained, equipped troops were already available at the threatened point.

The material condition of another offensive

German planners faced the corresponding problem of converting nominal resources into an effective concentration. The campaign study compiled for the U.S. Army records 409,998 personnel losses in the Russian theatre between 22 June and 31 August, against 217,000 replacements that had actually arrived by the latter date. These are theatre-wide figures for that defined period, not casualties in the Kiev battle alone. Their significance is the gap between losses and delivered replacements before September’s fighting had run its course. Men allocated on paper or expected later could not fill the places of those already absent.[1]

Equipment presented an additional constraint. Tanks undergoing repair, trucks awaiting parts and transport worn by repeated long movements limited what formations could do after they were reassigned. Reorientation required more than a new arrow on a headquarters map. Workshops and supply columns had to find their units, roads had to carry movement in the required direction, and the rail system had to deliver fuel and ammunition to usable unloading points. The forces gathering for another offensive were the products of the summer’s campaigning, with its accumulated wear and uneven replenishment.[1]

Guderian’s retrospective account describes a particularly revealing difficulty in preparing the next attack: supplies and replacements intended for his group were still being sent towards Orsha, associated with its earlier position, while it needed them farther south. His precise estimates should be read as a participant’s later account, but the underlying problem is concrete. An army could have supplies allocated to it and still lack them where the next operation required them. Previous movements left an administrative trail that had to be corrected as well as a physical distance that had to be covered.[6]g

These constraints also qualify claims that the turn towards Kiev alone cost Germany victory at Moscow. An August offensive against the capital would have required its own workable concentration, supplies and protection against Soviet forces on the flanks. The elapsed days cannot simply be transferred to an imagined uninterrupted advance. By late September, the historical choice was concrete: German leaders would attempt another offensive with formations whose losses and transport difficulties remained unresolved. Success at Kiev had changed the enemy’s position more dramatically than it had restored Germany’s own resources.

Moscow negotiates for the means to continue

On the Soviet side, international assistance was becoming a practical military question. The first formal meeting of the British, American and Soviet delegations in Moscow was scheduled for 29 September. W. Averell Harriman and Lord Beaverbrook had met Stalin and Molotov at the Kremlin the previous evening. The timing matters: while Germany was preparing to exploit its victory, the Soviet leadership was negotiating for resources with which to continue the war. These negotiations did not restore the armies lost at Kiev, but they demonstrate that the political and material struggle extended beyond the immediate battlefield.[7]h

The ambassadors leave the room

The Moscow negotiations opened with a small disturbance in diplomatic protocol. Steinhardt reported that, before the 28 September meeting, Beaverbrook asked Cripps to withdraw after the introductions; both ambassadors then left. Harriman later explained the request to Steinhardt as an attempt to overcome distrust between London and Moscow. That explanation was Harriman’s interpretation of Beaverbrook’s purpose, rather than proof of his private motives. The contemporary report shows how an urgent supply conference also depended on managing relationships among the people expected to negotiate it.[7]i

The discussions quickly became specific. In a telegram sent on 30 September, Harriman reported Stalin’s interest in light tanks carrying cannon and adequate armour, together with a particularly strong demand for antitank and antiaircraft guns. He also reported Stalin’s belief that German tank strength greatly exceeded Soviet strength. That statement records the Soviet leader’s assessment during negotiations; it is not an independently verified ratio of serviceable vehicles. The distinction preserves what the document actually tells us: the leadership’s perception of its material weakness and the categories of assistance it considered urgent.[8]

The agreement reached immediately afterward also exposed the distance between commitment and delivery. Reporting the conclusion on 1 October, Harriman stated that the American side would make the authorised supplies available, but that it had made no commitment on transportation, offering assistance instead. That qualification is central to the military history. Equipment had to be manufactured or released, moved to a port, carried through dangerous routes and distributed within the Soviet Union before a front could use it. Diplomacy could establish entitlement to supplies without solving every stage of their journey.[9]j

The conference also touched interests left unresolved by the invasion of Poland. On 8 September, the Polish ambassador in Washington requested representation because discussions with Moscow could affect Poland and the equipment of Polish forces being formed in Soviet territory. The American response kept the mission to its immediate military purpose and declined to add members. Fighting a shared enemy had not settled the consequences of the Soviet invasion or the future of the territories involved. The earlier history remains accessible in The Partition of Poland.[10]k

The occupation authorities organise murder

In Kiev, the German authorities were using their newly established control for a different purpose. The explosions and fires that began on 24 September, resulting from explosives left by Soviet forces, supplied a pretext for an attack on the city’s Jews. They did not establish collective Jewish responsibility. The decision to target an entire population, including children and elderly people, belonged to the occupiers. Describing the killings as a reprisal without that distinction would reproduce the perpetrators’ justification and obscure the nature of the crime.[11]

The perpetrators’ own records establish that the killing apparatus had arrived with the conquest. Operational Situation Report 106, dated 7 October, recorded an advance party of Sonderkommando 4a entering Kiev with the fighting troops on 19 September, followed by the main detachment on 25 September. Paul Blobel commanded the unit within Einsatzgruppe C. The record places its work beside that of the military authorities securing the city and dealing with demolitions. The machinery of persecution was therefore being established during the occupation’s first days, before the later report claimed that mass murder answered popular anger over the fires.[2]

Historian Kai Struve’s biographical study of Friedrich Jeckeln identifies the cooperation among Jeckeln, Einsatzgruppe C commander Otto Rasch and Kiev’s Wehrmacht commandant, Kurt Eberhard. Jeckeln, as Higher SS and Police Leader, connected the regional police apparatus with the killing units. Blobel’s Sonderkommando supplied a principal executing formation. This was an operation involving identifiable organisations and commanders, rather than an unexplained eruption of violence after a battle. The German Historical Museum also records discussions involving military officers, security police and Einsatzgruppe personnel before the massacre.[12][13]

Report 106 describes cooperation between the killing units and military authority. It says the assembly order was arranged with the city commandant and posted by the newly organised Ukrainian militia, and names Sonderkommando 4a, the Einsatzgruppe staff and two detachments of Police Regiment South in the killings. Its claim of military approval is part of the perpetrators’ record, to be assessed with other evidence. Authorising, organising, delivering notices, guarding and shooting were connected responsibilities whose attribution still requires attention to particular actions and commands.[2]l

The same record must be read critically when it describes the population. Its claims of general approval and its allegations about Jewish conduct served the killers’ explanation of their own actions. They cannot be treated as a representative survey of Kiev or as proof of the accusations. Local collaboration was real and requires examination, but collective guilt cannot be assigned to Ukrainians any more than Nazi accusations can establish collective guilt among Jews. Responsibility follows documented actions, positions and orders. The surviving record identifies German direction and auxiliary participation without making every resident an interchangeable participant.

The road to Babyn Yar

The order posted on 28 September required the Jews of Kiev and the surrounding area to assemble the next morning, bringing documents, valuables and clothing. Failure to appear was punishable by death.[14] Its demands made the rumour of removal plausible: possessions suitable for travel were requested, and the instruction presented obedience as the only lawful course. The threat and the deception worked together. People were being compelled to enter a system whose purpose was concealed from them, under conditions in which refusing the order also appeared lethal.[13][2]m

Dina Pronicheva accompanies her family

Dina Pronicheva told Soviet historians on 24 April 1946 why she accompanied relatives on 29 September. They expected deportation and needed help with sick and elderly family members; she left her children with her husband and joined them. She recalled barriers near the cemetery, the seizure of belongings and separation within the crowd. Taken to the killing place, she survived by falling among the bodies and later escaping. This was retrospective testimony. It traces how an act of family assistance became entrapment, and how one survivor could bear witness to people whose own accounts would never be recorded.[14]n

Pronicheva’s effort to escape also involved documents. She recalled discarding her identity card and presenting a trade-union card and work-book that did not state her nationality. Speaking Ukrainian, she persuaded a policeman that she had accompanied Jewish colleagues and should be released. He directed her to wait with another group. Her account then describes a German officer ordering that group’s execution to prevent witnesses from warning people still expected to arrive. A temporary acceptance of her claimed identity had not secured her safety. Her testimony connects an individual attempt to survive with the killers’ concern to conceal the operation while it continued. [14]o

The shootings continued on 30 September. Report 106 gave a total of 33,771 Jews murdered over 29–30 September together. This is the perpetrators’ reported figure for the two-day massacre, not a count for 29 September alone and not a total for all victims at Babyn Yar during the occupation. Further killings at the ravine would follow.[11][2]p

The possessions and the report

The German report described the money, valuables, clothing and linen taken from the victims, whose possessions had been seized before they were killed. Some goods were allocated through the Nazi welfare organisation for ethnic Germans, while others went to the city administration for distribution. Elsewhere the same report presented the apartments of murdered Jews as newly available housing for people displaced by the fires. The victims’ removal was thus translated into administrative benefits for others. Property transfer was not an incidental detail attached to the crime; it was one of the ways in which the occupation absorbed and normalised its consequences. [2]q

The report measured the operation by the perpetrators’ standards, describing little difficulty and claiming that knowledge of the killings remained limited. Its administrative language concealed extreme coercion and the suffering of the people murdered. The apartments presented as available housing had become vacant because their occupants were dead. Reading the record for evidence therefore also requires identifying what its account of successful administration leaves out.

Pronicheva also described violence absent from that administrative report. Hiding near the ravine the next morning, she said she saw German men rape and murder two women whom she identified as Jewish after hearing Yiddish. Her retrospective account does not name the assailants or establish a wider numerical pattern. It records the sexual violence she witnessed alongside the organised shootings, with the limits of that testimony kept attached to the episode.[14]r

The position reached

By 29 September, Germany could point to major territorial gains and the destruction of Soviet armies, but the strategic objectives that had shaped the invasion remained incompletely achieved. Leningrad had not fallen, Moscow remained beyond the German front, Odessa still resisted, and the Soviet government was assembling new military and international resources. German forces retained the capacity to inflict further disasters, yet their own losses and transport problems imposed limits that could not be removed by another declaration of confidence. The next offensive would begin with those contradictions already present.

Guderian’s attack began on 30 September, opening the next offensive towards Moscow. The killings at Babyn Yar continued that day. By the end of this phase, German armies had won a vast battle without ending Soviet resistance, while the occupation apparatus had demonstrated its capacity to destroy whole Jewish communities. Kamenets-Podolsk, Berdichev and Kiev reveal an escalation across the five weeks, not an atrocity suddenly detached from the campaign at its close. The next offensive began with Germany’s strategic purpose still unfulfilled and the human consequences of its conquests already irreversible. [1][2]s
